summary: Describes how certificate chains in TLS handshakes can be compressed, since they often make up most of the bytes sent. Compression cuts the amount of data and may avoid extra round trips. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: When your browser makes a secure connection, the website sends a bulky stack of ID papers. This document lets those papers be squeezed down so they travel faster.

questions: what is certificate compression in tls
which algorithms does tls certificate compression use
does certificate compression work with tls 1.2
subtitle: Shrinking the certificate chain in a TLS 1.3 handshake with zlib, Brotli or Zstandard.

tldr.problem: In TLS handshakes, certificate chains often take up most of the bytes transmitted. Earlier caching of certificates does not help on a first connection to a server.
tldr.mechanism: A new compress_certificate extension lists the compression algorithms a peer can decompress. The other side may then send a CompressedCertificate message in place of the Certificate message, using zlib, brotli or zstd.
tldr.outcome: Fewer bytes are sent and some round trips can be avoided. The extension works only with TLS 1.3 and newer. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 8879 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of TLS certificate compression.

sections.title: Why Compress Certificates
sections.content:
To reduce latency and improve performance, it helps to reduce the data exchanged during a TLS handshake. The abstract notes that certificate chains often take up the majority of the bytes transmitted.

RFC 7924 lets a client and server skip certificates already shared in an earlier handshake. It does not help when a client connects to a server for the first time. This document describes a mechanism that lets certificates be compressed during all handshakes.
sections.eli5: The website has to show a big pile of ID papers every time. Squishing the pile into a smaller packet means it arrives sooner.

sections.title: Negotiating Compression
sections.content:
The extension is only supported with TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) and newer. If TLS 1.2 or earlier is negotiated, the peers MUST ignore it.

The new extension type is compress_certificate(27). When a client sends it in the ClientHello, it says it can handle compressed server certificates. When a server sends it in a CertificateRequest, it says it can handle compressed client certificates.

The extension data is a list of CertificateCompressionAlgorithm values the sender is willing to use for decompression: zlib(1), brotli(2) and zstd(3). The extension is a one-way indication, and no response extension is needed.
sections.eli5: Each side tells the other which kinds of squishing it knows how to undo. Nobody has to answer; they just say it once.

sections.title: The CompressedCertificate Message
sections.content:
If the peer has indicated support, a server or client MAY compress its Certificate message and send it as a CompressedCertificate message that replaces the Certificate message. The message has three fields.

  • algorithm: the algorithm used. It MUST be one the peer listed in its compress_certificate extension.
  • uncompressed_length: the length of the Certificate message once uncompressed. If it does not match the real length after decompression, the receiver MUST abort with the bad_certificate alert. It also lets the receiver preallocate a buffer and enforce size limits before decompressing.
  • compressed_certificate_message: the compressed encoding of the Certificate message that would have been sent without compression.

For zlib the message MUST use RFC 1950, for brotli RFC 7932, and for zstd RFC 8478. If the message cannot be decompressed, the connection MUST be terminated with the bad_certificate alert. If the certificate format was altered using the server_certificate_type or client_certificate_type extensions (RFC 7250), the altered message is what gets compressed.
sections.eli5: The sender puts the squished papers in an envelope marked with the squishing method and the original size. If the size does not match after unsquishing, the receiver hangs up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
After decompression, the Certificate message MUST be processed as if it had been sent uncompressed, so parsing and verification keep their usual security properties. Because certificate chains are typically presented per server name or per user, a malicious application has no control over individual fragments of the message and cannot leak information about the certificate by changing the plaintext.

Implementations SHOULD bound memory use when decompressing. They MUST limit the decompressed chain to the stated uncompressed length and MUST abort if the output exceeds it. TLS framing imposes a 16777216-byte limit on certificate messages, and implementations may set a lower one, applying the same limit as without compression.

Third parties can infer things from the length of the encrypted Certificate message. Compression changes that length in a way that depends on the certificate contents, so any padding scheme covering the message has to account for compression or disable it.
sections.eli5: When the papers are unsquished they must be checked just like normal ones. And the receiver must not let a tiny envelope blow up into a giant pile.

sections.title: Middlebox Compatibility
sections.content:
A significant number of middleboxes intercept and try to validate the Certificate message during a TLS handshake. Ones that do not understand CompressedCertificate might misbehave and drop connections that use it.

For that reason the extension is only supported where the certificate message is encrypted in a way that stops middleboxes from intercepting it, which means TLS 1.3 and higher.
sections.eli5: Some old gatekeepers on the road peek at the papers and get confused by a squished packet. In TLS 1.3 the papers are sealed so they cannot peek.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA created compress_certificate(27) in the "TLS ExtensionType Values" registry, with the TLS 1.3 column set to "CH, CR" and Recommended set to "Yes". It also created compressed_certificate(25) in the "TLS Handshake Type" registry with DTLS-OK set to "Yes".

The RFC creates a new registry, "TLS Certificate Compression Algorithm IDs". Values below 256 are allocated by IETF Review, values 256 to 16383 by Specification Required, and the rest is for Experimental Use. Algorithm 0 is reserved, and 16384 to 65535 is reserved for experimental use.
sections.eli5: The official lists of numbers get new entries, and a new list is started for the squishing methods.
